docs.title: Sprint 1 Summary
docs.text:
Sprint 1 delivers the core logbook functionality with authentication and user management:

  • Authentication — Registration, login, JWT tokens, email verification, password reset, and account deletion.
  • Two-Factor Authentication — TOTP-based 2FA with QR code setup, enable/disable flow in Settings.
  • Project Management — Create, edit, archive/unarchive projects with unique name enforcement per user.
  • Entry Schema Definition — Define custom entry fields (TEXT, NUMBER, DATE, BOOLEAN) per project.
  • Entry CRUD — Create, update, delete logbook entries with typed field values, due dates, and backdated entry dates.
  • Time Tracking — Record duration per entry, view per-project time summaries (total hours, entry count, last entry).
  • Dashboard — Greeting, stat cards (active projects, entries this week, total time), SVG activity sparkline chart, current projects list, and recent entries table.
  • Project Detail View — Entry format section (required/optional indicators), grouped entries by date, clean modal form for entry creation.
  • Entry Browser — Vertical timeline layout with date grouping, search, project filter, entry type filter (All/This Week/Overdue), and newest/oldest sort toggle.
  • Overdue Entries — Entries past due_date flagged with red border, warning badge, and dedicated Overdue filter tab.
  • Profile Page — Avatar upload, bio/slogan, degree, year, and student number with edit mode.
  • Settings — Account management, 2FA setup, dark/light theme, notification preferences, logbook preferences, and data export/import (JSON/CSV).
  • Auth UI — Full-screen animated canvas background with floating particles, light streaks, and logbook icons. Frosted-glass form cards.
  • API Testing — 27 Vitest integration tests covering all endpoints against the live database.
  • Responsive Design — Tailwind CSS v4 design system with dark mode, collapsible sidebar, and mobile-friendly layout.

docs.title: Sprint 2 Summary
docs.text:
Sprint 2 builds on the Sprint 1 foundation (authentication, project management, entry CRUD, dashboard, and settings) with richer entry formatting, deeper analytics, offline support, and cross-feature integration.

  • Rich Field Types — Support for tags, checklists, links, and references as entry field types, extending the original TEXT/NUMBER/DATE/BOOLEAN set.
  • Entry Format Editing — Add, remove, and rename fields on an existing project's entry format after creation.
  • Entry Format Versioning — Preserve previous versions of an entry format so historical entries remain valid and readable after schema changes.
  • Computed Fields — Define fields whose values are calculated automatically from other fields in the same entry.
  • Custom Field Analytics — Totals, grouping, comparisons, and plotting/visualization of data captured in custom fields.
  • Alternative Views — Calendar view and board (kanban-style) view for browsing entries beyond the existing timeline layout.
  • Unfinished Work & Due Date Tracking — Dedicated tracking for outstanding/unfinished entries and their due dates, building on Sprint 1's overdue flagging.
  • Offline Entry Capture — Create and save entries locally without a connection, with sync to the server once back online.
  • Data Export & Import (Extended) — Expanded export/import functionality for logbook data, building on Sprint 1's JSON/CSV support.
  • Cross-Feature Integration & Testing — Integration of all Sprint 2 features into a cohesive whole, end-to-end testing across features, resolution of cross-feature bugs, and regression testing against Sprint 1 functionality.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• User: UNIQUE(email) — each email can only register once.
  • Project: UNIQUE(userId, name) — a student cannot have two projects with the same name.
  • EntryValue: UNIQUE(entryId, fieldId) — one value per field per entry.
  • All foreign keys use ON DELETE CASCADE for full account erasure.

docs.title: 7. Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)
docs.text:
The app supports optional TOTP-based two-factor authentication using otplib (v13) and qrcode:

  • Enable 2FA: Backend generates a TOTP secret and QR code URI. User scans the QR code with an authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy, etc.).
  • Verify 2FA: User provides a 6-digit TOTP code which is verified against the stored secret.
  • Disable 2FA: User confirms with their password to disable 2FA and clear the stored secret.
  • Scheduled Deletion: Users can schedule their account for deletion, which is tracked via the scheduledDeletionAt field on the User model.

The 2FA secret is stored in the twoFactorSecret column on the User model. The isTwoFactorEnabled boolean flag controls whether 2FA is enforced at login.

docs.title: 8. Shared Types Package
docs.text:
The @logbook/shared package (packages/shared/src/index.ts) exports TypeScript types, Zod schemas, and interfaces consumed by both frontend and backend:

  • Project, ProjectWithFields
  • EntryField, EntryFieldType
  • Entry, EntryFieldValue
  • TimeSummary
  • CreateProjectInput, UpdateProjectInput
  • CreateEntryInput, UpdateEntryInput
  • CreateEntryFieldInput
  • Auth schemas: registerSchema, loginSchema, verifyEmailSchema, forgotPasswordSchema, resetPasswordSchema, deleteAccountSchema
  • ApiError

This eliminates type duplication and ensures the frontend and backend agree on data shapes.

docs.title: Client Interaction Logs
docs.text: This document tracks requirements, Q&A, and decisions made in consultation with the client (lecturers/TAs). It serves as project methodology evidence and records how client feedback influenced the development of the Digital Logbook.

docs.title: [Date: 2026-08-13] — Project Process & Evidence Feedback
docs.text:

  • The team must document its Kanban project methodology.

docs.title: [Date: 2026-08-17] — Requirements Clarification Meeting
docs.text:
• Channel: Requirements Review Meeting.

  • Attendees: Client / Lecturer, Development Team (all members).

docs.title: 1. Project Ownership & Naming
docs.text:
• Client Decision: A project is strictly owned by a single student. Project names must be unique for each student (e.g., a student cannot have two projects named "CS Lab 1").

  • Impact:

  • projects table uses user_id UUID REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE.

  • Unique constraint: UNIQUE(user_id, name).

docs.title: 2. Project Archiving Behavior (US05)
docs.text:
• Client Decision: Archiving a project does not lock it into a read-only state. Users can still create new entries, edit/delete existing entries, and unarchive the project at any time.

  • Impact: Archiving is implemented as a UI/filtering state (status = 'ARCHIVED') rather than a backend permission lock. This is handled through PATCH /api/projects/:id/status.

docs.title: 3. Time Tracking, Live Timer & Overdue Flagging (US04)
docs.text:
• Client Decision:

  • Time tracking on logbook entries is mandatory.

  • The system must include a live timer feature for recording entry duration.

  • Entries/tasks must support flagging items as overdue.

  • Impact:

  • logbook_entries requires duration_minutes INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.

  • logbook_entries includes due_date TIMESTAMP to support overdue calculations.
  • logbook_entries includes entry_date TIMESTAMP to support backdating.
  • The frontend requires a live stopwatch/timer widget that calculates elapsed time.

docs.title: 4. Entry Editing & Account Erasure
docs.text:
• Client Decision: Logbook entries can be edited and deleted after creation. When an account is deleted, all user data, projects, and entries must be permanently erased.

  • Impact: Foreign keys enforce ON DELETE CASCADE where appropriate. This behaviour was verified in the Prisma schema.

docs.title: 5. Stats, Analytics & External API Integration
docs.text:
• Client Decision:

  • The system must include project statistics and analytics.

  • The external API integration should use a Calendar API, such as syncing logbook deadlines or entries to an external calendar.

  • Impact:

  • Backend provides GET /api/projects/:id/time-summary for per-project time aggregates.

  • The Dashboard provides cross-project statistics.
  • Calendar integration was identified as a future development requirement.

docs.title: 6. Entry Timestamps & Backdating
docs.text:
• Client Decision: The handling of entry timestamps was left to engineering discretion.

  • Engineering Decision: Include both created_at (system audit timestamp) and entry_date (user-customisable timestamp) on entries. This allows students to backdate work while maintaining an audit record.

docs.title: [Date: 2026-08-21] — Sprint Review & Rubric Compliance Check
docs.text:
• Channel: In-person sprint review meeting with client/lecturer.

  • Attendees: Client / Lecturer, Development Team (Dineo Motloung, Athandwa, Alondwe and Wendy).

docs.title: Meeting Context
docs.text: The client conducted a review of the project against the assessment rubric, checking the implementation status of the required features. The team presented the current state of the application, including authentication, project management, entry CRUD, time tracking, dashboard, profile, and settings.

docs.title: 1. Authentication — Confirmed as Core Requirement
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client confirmed that authentication, including user registration, login, email verification, and password reset, is an explicit rubric requirement and must not be treated as optional or deferred.

  • Status: Fully implemented — JWT-based authentication with registration, login, email verification, password reset, and account deletion.

  • Client Feedback: The client was satisfied with the implementation. Temporary development-mode auto-verification was considered acceptable during development, but production deployment should enforce real email verification.

docs.title: 2. Due Dates & Overdue Flagging — Non-Negotiable
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client reconfirmed that due dates and overdue flagging are mandatory requirements.

  • Decisions:

  • Every logbook entry must support a due_date field.

  • Entries past their due date must be automatically identified as overdue.
  • The UI must provide an Overdue section/filter alongside other entry views.

  • Overdue entries must be visually distinguished.

  • Impact:

  • logbook_entries.due_date is included in the Prisma schema.

  • Overdue status is determined using the entry due date and completion status.
  • The Entries and Project Detail views support overdue filtering.
  • The Dashboard includes overdue information.

docs.title: 3. Live Timer / Stopwatch for Time Tracking
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client emphasised that time tracking should go beyond manually entering a duration. A live stopwatch feature was identified as a required improvement.

  • Decisions:

  • The entry creation/edit form should include a live stopwatch.

  • The stopwatch should support start, pause, and reset.
  • The timer should measure elapsed time and convert it to the required duration value when saved.

  • Users should still be able to enter a duration manually.

  • Impact:

  • A stopwatch component was developed for the entry form.

  • Timer state is persisted during the active session to reduce the risk of losing timing information.
  • The existing duration_minutes backend field supports the saved duration.

docs.title: 4. Overdue Reminders & Notifications
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client asked about reminder capabilities for approaching deadlines.

  • Decisions:

  • The system should support advance reminders, such as reminders three days before, one day before, and on the due date.

  • In-app notifications are sufficient for the current implementation.

  • Email notifications are not required for the initial implementation.

  • Impact:

  • Deadline reminders were implemented in the application.

  • A notification indicator was added to provide users with visibility of notifications.
  • The existing due-date information is used to determine when reminders should be displayed.

docs.title: 5. Calendar API Integration (External API)
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client reconfirmed the requirement for an external API integration. The team proposed Calendar API synchronisation as the most natural integration for a digital logbook.

  • Decisions:

  • Logbook due dates should be exportable or synchronisable to an external calendar.

  • Google Calendar was identified as the preferred integration.

  • Calendar synchronisation was planned for a later development phase.

  • Impact:

  • The existing due_date field provides the required data for calendar events.

  • Google Calendar API integration requires OAuth2 configuration and external service credentials.
  • This feature remains planned for future development.

docs.title: 6. Per-Project Time Recording with Stopwatch
docs.text:
• Discussion: The client asked about recording the total amount of time spent on individual projects.

  • Decisions:

  • Per-project total time should be calculated from the durations of the project's entries.

  • Time recorded using the stopwatch contributes to the relevant entry duration.

  • Project totals should be clearly visible to users.

  • Impact:

  • The existing GET /api/projects/:id/time-summary endpoint provides project-level time aggregation.

  • The Project Detail page can use this information to display cumulative project time.

docs.title: 7. Rubric Compliance Check
docs.text:
The client reviewed the following rubric areas:

docs.title: 1.1 Methodology Used
docs.text:
We use a Kanban-based methodology with individual functional-area ownership rather than a traditional fixed-length Scrum sprint model.

The project is organised into functional areas, with user stories assigned to team members according to the relationships and dependencies between features.

For Sprint 1 – Core Logbook, the user stories were distributed as follows:

Team Member User Stories Functional Area Person 1 US00.1, US00.2, US00.3, US00.4 Authentication & Account Management Person 2 US01, US05 Project Management Person 3 US02, US03 Entry Structure & Entry Creation Person 4 US04, US06 Time Tracking & Entry Browsing

Work flows through a single shared Kanban board with columns:

Backlog → To Do → In Progress → Done

Each team member manages the flow of their assigned stories while coordinating with other members when cross-area dependencies arise.

For the Intermediate phase, work was divided into four functional areas:

Team Member User Stories Functional Area Person 1 US07, US08, US09, US10 Entry Formats & Fields Person 2 US11, US12, US13 Statistics & Views Person 3 US14, US15 Offline & Data Person 4 Integration & Testing Cross-feature Integration

docs.title: 1.2 Reasoning & Motivation
docs.text:
• Why Kanban instead of Scrum: The project contains features with clear functional dependencies rather than work that must always be completed simultaneously within a fixed sprint. Kanban allows team members to progress their assigned functionality while making dependencies visible.

The core dependency chain established during Sprint 1 was:

$$ \text{Authentication} \longrightarrow \text{Projects} \longrightarrow \text{Entry Formats} \longrightarrow \text{Entries} \longrightarrow \text{Time Tracking / Browsing} $$

The Intermediate phase builds on this foundation by extending entry formats and adding functionality that operates across existing logbook data:

$$ \text{Entry Formats} \longrightarrow \text{Rich Fields / Computed Fields} \longrightarrow \text{Statistics / Views} \longrightarrow \text{Offline / Data Portability} $$

  • Functional Ownership: Related stories are assigned to the same developer where possible. For example, US07–US10 are closely related because they all extend the entry-format system. Keeping these stories together allows one developer to maintain consistency between field definitions, format changes, versioning, and computed values.

  • Handling Cross-Area Dependencies: We use a status:blocked-on-dependency label. A story waiting on an upstream dependency remains in Backlog with this label. Once the required contract, schema, or functionality is available, the label is removed and the issue can move to To Do.

  • Commits and Pull Requests referenced issue numbers using references such as closes #7.
  • Work was tracked through the Gitea Kanban board.

For the Intermediate phase:

  • User stories US07–US15 were defined and assigned according to functional area.
  • Intermediate work was tracked using the same Kanban-based workflow.
  • Features were integrated with the existing Sprint 1 functionality rather than implemented as isolated components.
  • Testing was performed across the new functionality and its interaction with the existing system.

docs.title: 3.1 Sprint 1 – What Went Well
docs.text:
• Vertical slice delivery: All 10 core user stories from authentication through time tracking and entry browsing were implemented as end-to-end vertical slices covering the database, API, and UI.

  • Shared types package: Extracting types into @logbook/shared eliminated duplication and helped identify type mismatches between the frontend and backend early.

  • Integration testing: 27 Vitest tests running against the Neon database provided confidence that API endpoints worked correctly, including edge cases such as duplicate names, missing resources, and invalid input.

  • Prisma ORM adoption: Migrating from raw SQL to Prisma simplified database access and provided type-safe queries.

  • Kanban workflow: The dependency-chain model worked well with functional ownership and made dependencies between areas visible to the team.

docs.title: 3.2 Intermediate Phase – What Went Well
docs.text:
• Feature ownership: Grouping related Intermediate stories by functional area helped maintain consistency between related features.

  • Extension of the existing system: The Intermediate features were developed on top of the Sprint 1 foundation rather than requiring a separate system.

  • Integration and testing: Dedicated integration work helped identify issues occurring between independently developed features and ensured that the new functionality continued to work with existing features.

  • Flexible entry model: Extending the entry-format system with richer fields and computed values moved the project closer to the specification's requirement for customisable logbook entries.

docs.title: 3.3 What Could Be Improved
docs.text:
• Frontend error handling: The frontend uses basic error banners for API failures. A proper toast notification system would improve the user experience.

  • Test isolation: Integration tests run against the live database without transaction rollback. Tests create and clean up data, but parallel test runs could potentially conflict.

  • Documentation gaps: Some documentation was written towards the end of development rather than incrementally. Future work should update documentation alongside implementation.

  • Cross-feature integration: As more Intermediate features were introduced, dependencies between features became more complex. Earlier integration of completed components would reduce the risk of discovering compatibility issues near the end of development.

Although the Intermediate user stories have been completed, several improvements identified from client feedback remain useful for further development:

  1. Add frontend toast notifications for API errors.
  2. Add unit tests alongside integration tests for complex business logic.
  3. Add Calendar API integration where required.
  4. Improve the visual presentation of overdue entries.
  5. Add a live stopwatch widget to entry creation/editing.
  6. Surface per-project cumulative time more prominently on the Project Detail page.
  7. Improve notification and deadline-reminder functionality.

These items are treated as future improvements rather than incomplete Intermediate user stories.

Create apps/backend/.env from the example file:

cp apps/backend/.env.example apps/backend/.env

Edit apps/backend/.env and set the following variables:

docs.title: 5. Set up the database schema
docs.text:
The backend uses Prisma 7 with a prisma.config.ts file that reads the DATABASE_URL from your .env. All Prisma commands must be run from inside the apps/backend/ directory:

cd apps/backend
npx prisma generate
npx prisma db push

This creates all tables (users, projects, entry_fields, entries, password_resets) in your Neon database. Use npx prisma db push --force-reset if you need to clear existing data during development.

docs.title: 6. Run development servers
docs.text:
You need both servers running simultaneously:

Terminal 1 — Backend (Express API on port 3000):

npm run dev --workspace=backend

Terminal 2 — Frontend (Vite dev server on port 5173):

npm run dev --workspace=frontend

The frontend proxies /api/* requests to http://localhost:3000 via the Vite config.

Open http://localhost:5173 in your browser to use the app.

Note: Both servers must be running. Without the backend, all API calls return a 502 Bad Gateway.

docs.title: Authentication & Email
docs.text:
The app uses JWT-based authentication with email verification and optional two-factor authentication (2FA):

  • Registration creates a user with an unverified email
  • Email verification — a verification link is sent via Gmail SMTP (if configured)
  • Login is blocked until the email is verified
  • Password reset — reset link sent via email
  • Two-factor authentication (2FA) — TOTP-based 2FA using otplib. Users can enable/disable 2FA in Settings. When enabled, a QR code is generated for authenticator app setup.

Dev mode (no Gmail credentials): accounts are automatically verified so you can develop without email setup. The verification link is logged to the backend console.

Production mode: set GMAIL_USER and GMAIL_APP_PASSWORD in .env to enable real email sending.

All commits must follow Conventional Commits format:

<type>: <description>

[optional body]

Common types: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: This page documents how the Digital Logbook is tested: our test stack and why we chose it, what is covered by automated tests, the formal user feedback process, our testing policy, and proof of passing runs.

docs.title: Test Stack & Why We Chose It
docs.text:
Tool Role Why Vitest 4 Test runner and assertion framework Same engine that powers our frontend build tooling (Vite), so one dependency ecosystem covers the whole monorepo. Fast, ESM-native, and watch-mode works out of the box with TypeScript — no extra transpile config. Supertest HTTP-level request helper (backend) Lets tests call the Express app directly (request(app).post(...)) without starting a real server or opening a port. We test the real HTTP layer — routing, middleware, validation, status codes, JSON bodies — not just functions. React Testing Library Component testing (frontend) Tests components the way users interact with them — finding elements by placeholder text, role, and label rather than by implementation details like CSS class or component state. jsdom Browser environment for frontend tests Provides a lightweight DOM inside Node.js so React components can render, fire events, and validate forms without a real browser. The real Express app (src/app.ts) System under test (backend) The app module is exported separately from the server entry point (src/index.ts) precisely so tests can import it without binding port 3000. Live PostgreSQL (Neon) Real database (backend) Integration tests run against the actual database the app uses, exercising real Prisma queries, real constraints (unique, cascade deletes), and real SQL aggregation. Mocking Prisma would test our mocks, not our app. otplib TOTP code generation in tests The 2FA tests generate genuinely valid time-based codes with the same library the server uses to verify them, so the full TOTP round-trip is tested end-to-end.

Testing pyramid: the backend has integration tests (API-level, real database) and unit tests (pure functions); the frontend has component tests (rendered React components with jsdom) and unit tests (pure logic like saved-filter persistence).

docs.title: 1. Core API (api.test.ts — 27 tests)
docs.text:
• Health and database connectivity
  • Project CRUD: create, list, read, update, archive/unarchive, 404/409/400 error paths
  • Entry fields: creation per type, listing, inclusion in project reads
  • Entries: creation with/without dates, update, delete, time-summary aggregation

docs.title: 2. Authentication & Security (auth.test.ts — 29 tests)
docs.text:
• Registration: happy path, duplicate email (409), weak password (400), invalid email (400)
  • Login: valid credentials return a JWT; wrong password and unknown email both return the identical error (no account enumeration); unverified accounts blocked with 403
  • Route protection: missing token → 401, invalid token → 401
  • 2FA full lifecycle, in order: status check → setup (secret + QR data URL) → wrong code rejected → valid code enables → already-enabled rejected → login returns requiresTwoFactor with no token → /login/2fa rejects bad code, accepts valid code and issues JWT, rejects malformed code → disable rejects wrong password → disable with correct password → login back to normal
  • Password reset: anti-enumeration behaviour (same message for known and unknown emails), invalid token rejected (400), full end-to-end reset (old password stops working, new one works, all reset tokens consumed)
  • Account deletion: wrong password rejected; correct password permanently erases the user

docs.title: How the Tests Work
docs.text:
Backend API test — a real HTTP request to the real Express app backed by the real database:

it("PATCH /entries/:id/status marks entry DONE and sets completedAt", async () => {
  const res = await request(app)          // real Express app, no port
    .patch(`/api/entries/${statusEntryId}/status`)
    .set(H)                                // Authorization: Bearer <real JWT>
    .send({ status: "DONE" });

  expect(res.status).toBe(200);
  expect(res.body.status).toBe("DONE");
  expect(res.body.completedAt).not.toBeNull();
});

Frontend component test — renders the real React component in jsdom and asserts on DOM output:

it("renders the session-expired banner when the URL has ?expired=1", () => {
  window.history.pushState({}, "", "/login?expired=1");
  renderLoginPage();
  expect(screen.getByText(/session expired/i)).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Backend unit test — exercises pure functions directly:

it("verifyToken returns null for a tampered token", () => {
  const token = generateToken("user-1");
  const tampered = token.slice(0, -1) + (token.endsWith("A") ? "B" : "A");
  expect(verifyToken(tampered)).toBeNull();
});

Shared conventions across test files:

  • Own user per file (backend). Each suite creates its own test user (unique UUID + timestamped email), so suites never collide even though Vitest runs test files in parallel.
  • Setup in beforeAll, cleanup via cascade (backend). Fixed data is created once; afterAll deletes the test user and every foreign key is ON DELETE CASCADE.
  • Sequential within a suite where one test's output feeds the next (the 2FA lifecycle).
  • API modules mocked at the boundary (frontend). Frontend component tests mock ../api so they test the UI layer in isolation from the backend.
  • 15s per-test timeout for backend tests — the database is remote (Neon), so round-trips cost ~500ms each.

docs.title: How to Run Them
docs.text:
# Backend tests (from the repository root)
npm run test --workspace=apps/backend

# Frontend tests
npm run test --workspace=apps/frontend

# Watch mode (re-runs on file changes)
npm run test:watch --workspace=apps/backend
npm run test:watch --workspace=apps/frontend

Backend prerequisites: a reachable DATABASE_URL in apps/backend/.env and a regenerated Prisma client (npx prisma generate in apps/backend — see Bugs Found By Testing).

Email behaviour in tests: with no SMTP credentials configured, registration auto-verifies (dev mode) and password-reset emails fail silently — both are caught and logged, and the endpoints still behave correctly. The tests assert the HTTP contract, never the email delivery.

docs.title: Testing Policy
docs.text:
1. Every API endpoint gets tests for the happy path and its error paths (400 validation, 401 auth, 404 missing, 409 conflict). If an endpoint has no error-path test, it isn't done.
  2. Never mock what we're testing at the integration level. No Prisma mocks, no stub auth. The database is real; failures must be real failures. Unit tests for pure functions may use mocks for external dependencies.
  3. Security behaviour is tested as behaviour, not implementation — e.g. we assert that unknown-email and wrong-password logins return byte-identical errors, not that some flag was set.
  4. Tests must clean up after themselves via user-cascade deletion, so the shared database stays usable.
  5. Regression rule: any bug found (see below) gets a test that would have caught it before the fix is considered done.
  6. Tests run in CI before every merge to main — a red suite blocks the merge. The Gitea Actions workflow runs both backend and frontend test suites on every push to protected branches.

docs.title: User Feedback Process
docs.text:
Automated testing checks what the code does; user feedback checks whether it works for real users. Our formal process:

  1. Instrument: a standard SUS (System Usability Scale) questionnaire — 10 fixed Likert items, scored 0–100 — so results are quantifiable and comparable across rounds.
  2. Scenario-based sessions: each tester gets the same set of task scenarios (register → create project → add entry → mark done → view stats/calendar → enable 2FA). We record pass/fail per task and where testers hesitate.
  3. Recruitment: 5–8 testers per round — classmates, other teams, and our client.
  4. Analysis & integration: SUS scores and task failures are reviewed as a team; each actionable finding becomes an issue on the tracker with an assigned fix, and fixed items are reported back in the next round.
  5. Records: each round is logged in docs/user-feedback.md with the raw scores, findings, and the feedback → action → commit trail.

The first formal round is scheduled for Sprint 2; results will be published on this site.

docs.title: Bugs Found By Testing
docs.text:
Writing these tests surfaced two real issues — this is the regression rule in action:

  1. Stale Prisma client broke every entry-creation test (11 pre-existing failures). The generated client predated the Sprint 2 schema, so any query touching entry_fields.archived_at threw PrismaClientValidationError: Unknown argument archivedAt. Fix: run npx prisma generate after pulling schema changes. Lesson: prisma generate belongs in postinstall/CI.

  2. Concurrent entry-field creation can race on format versioning. Each field create does read-latest-version → insert latest+1. Two parallel creates both read version N and both try to insert N+1; the unique (project_id, version) constraint rejects one, so one field creation fails with 400. Tests create fields sequentially (matching real UI usage). Fix candidate: wrap version bump in a transaction with a retry, or use MAX(version)+1 inside a serializable transaction. Both are filed on the issue tracker.

docs.title: Third-Party Code
docs.text:
This page documents every third-party library and external service the Digital Logbook depends on, and — more importantly — why each one was chosen. Our policy is to lean on well-maintained, permissively licensed libraries for solved problems (authentication primitives, email, build tooling) while hand-writing everything that is core to the product (the REST API, business logic, database schema and UI components).

Every package below is declared in package.json (per workspace) and its license was verified from the installed package.json on disk.

docs.title: How we evaluate dependencies
docs.text:
Before adding a library we check:

  1. Fit — does it solve a problem we would otherwise hand-roll poorly (crypto, date handling, bundling)?
  2. Maintenance — is it actively maintained and widely adopted?
  3. License — permissive (MIT / BSD / Apache-2.0) so it is safe for a university project; no copyleft surprises.
  4. Size — is the dependency worth its footprint on the bundle?

Schema-as-code also gives us reviewable migrations. @prisma/adapter-pg ^7.9 Apache-2.0 Driver adapter for PostgreSQL Prisma's driver-adapter pattern lets us bring our own pg connection pool, which is the recommended way to talk to Neon's serverless Postgres over a pooled connection string. pg ^8.23 MIT PostgreSQL wire-protocol driver Required by the Prisma adapter; a mature, battle-tested driver. zod ^4.4 MIT Schema validation One validation library shared by frontend and backend through @logbook/shared — the same Zod schema validates the register form in React and the request body on the server. docs.title: User Feedback
docs.text: This page documents the formal user feedback process we use to improve the Digital Logbook. Feedback is collected through a standardised instrument — the System Usability Scale (SUS) — combined with task-scenario observations and open-ended responses. Findings are tracked and every actionable change is recorded in the integration table at the bottom of this page.

docs.title: Why we collect feedback
docs.text: Automated tests verify that the code does what we intend; user feedback verifies that the product works for the people it's for. The feedback process is a required part of our methodology: every round of collection is followed by a round of integration, where each actionable finding becomes a tracked issue with an assigned fix.

docs.title: The formal process
docs.text: Stage What happens Instrument A Google Form with the 10 standard SUS items, 7 task-completion self-reports, and open-ended questions. Testers 5–8 per round: classmates, members of other teams, and our client (where available). Demographics are captured in the form itself. Session format 15–20 minutes, supervised. The tester works through the 7 task scenarios on the live app while an observer notes pass/fail and friction points on the observation sheet below. Recording Form responses land in a linked Google Sheet. An observer's written notes are kept alongside as a second data source. Analysis SUS scores per tester (0–100) and an average across the round; per-task pass/fail counts; open-ended responses grouped by theme. Integration Every actionable finding becomes an issue on the bug tracker with an owner and a fix commit. The integration table below records the full trail.

docs.title: The feedback form
docs.text:
Link: https://forms.gle/g4gEzYtiFRSXCQ5CA

The form is structured in four sections:

  1. Welcome & About You — consent statement, role (Student / Lecturer or tutor / Working professional / Other), and prior experience with digital logbooks or work-tracking tools.
  2. Task Feedback — for each of 7 tasks (register, create project, add entry, mark done, view stats, view calendar/board, enable 2FA), the tester self-reports Completed easily / Completed with some difficulty / Could not complete, plus an optional comment field per task.
  3. System Usability Scale — the 10 standard SUS items on a 5-point Likert scale (Strongly disagree → Strongly agree). Worded verbatim; the SUS instrument is free to use and publicly cited across HCI research.
  4. Open Feedback — most frustrating part (required), favourite feature, one-thing-to-change, and an NPS-style 0–10 recommend-likelihood scale.

A screenshot of the published form is captured after each round. The raw response data for each round is stored as a CSV file in this repository (e.g. docs/user-feedback-round1.csv).

docs.text:
Self-reported answers are one half of the evidence; the other half is what the observer actually sees. For each session, fill in this table on paper alongside the tester:

Task Completed Notes / friction points 1. Register a new account ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 2. Log in and create a project with custom fields ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 3. Add a logbook entry (with duration + due date) ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 4. Mark an entry as done ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 5. Check project statistics (totals, averages) ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 6. Find calendar and board views ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌ 7. Enable two-factor authentication ✅ / ⚠️ / ❌

✅ = completed easily · ⚠️ = completed with difficulty · ❌ = could not complete.

docs.title: SUS scoring (in the linked Google Sheet)
docs.text:
When the form is linked to a Google Sheet (Responses → create spreadsheet), add these helper columns to auto-score each row:

Column Header Formula SUS_1 q1_adj =B2-1 (odd item: subtract 1) SUS_2 q2_adj =5-C2 (even item: 5 − answer) SUS_3 q3_adj =D2-1 SUS_4 q4_adj =5-E2 SUS_5 q5_adj =F2-1 SUS_6 q6_adj =5-G2 SUS_7 q7_adj =H2-1 SUS_8 q8_adj =5-I2 SUS_9 q9_adj =J2-1 SUS_10 q10_adj =5-K2 SUS score =SUM(q1_adj:q10_adj) * 2.5 (yields 0–100)

Adjust column letters to match the actual sheet columns produced by the grid question. The pattern — odd items score answer − 1, even items score 5 − answer, then sum and multiply by 2.5 — is the canonical SUS calculation from Brooke (1996).

Average SUS across the round: =AVERAGE(SUS_score_range). Industry benchmarks (Sauro, 2011) place the average SUS at 68/100; anything above ~72 is above-average, above ~80 is excellent.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook is designed as a non-monolithic web application consisting of a React frontend, an Express backend, and a PostgreSQL database.

The frontend communicates with the backend through a hand-written REST API. The backend handles business logic, authentication, validation, and database access.

docs.title: High-Level Architecture
docs.text:
┌─────────────────┐       HTTP/REST        ┌─────────────────┐
│                  │  ───────────────────►  │                  │
│    Frontend      │                        │    Backend       │
│   React + Vite   │  ◄───────────────────  │   Express API    │
│   TypeScript     │     JSON responses     │   TypeScript     │
│   Tailwind CSS   │                        │   Prisma ORM     │
│                  │                        │                  │
└─────────────────┘                        └────────┬─────────┘
                                                    │
                                           Prisma / pg driver
                                                    │
                                           ┌────────▼─────────┐
                                           │                  │
                                           │   PostgreSQL     │
                                           │   (Neon hosted)  │
                                           │                  │
                                           └──────────────────┘

The frontend is a single-page application served by Vite during development and as static files in production. The backend is a standalone Express server. They communicate exclusively through JSON over HTTP.

docs.title: Separation of Concerns
docs.text:
Layer Responsibility Technology Presentation UI rendering, user interaction, client-side routing React 19, Tailwind CSS v4 API Request handling, authentication, validation, business logic Express 5, Zod, JWT Data Access Type-safe database queries, migrations Prisma ORM 7 Persistence Relational data storage PostgreSQL (Neon) Shared Common types and validation schemas @logbook/shared

The frontend never accesses the database directly. All data flows through the backend API, ensuring consistent validation and authentication enforcement.

docs.title: Authentication Flow
docs.text:
┌──────────┐    POST /api/auth/register     ┌──────────┐
│  Client   │  ──────────────────────────►   │ Backend  │
│  (React)  │                                │          │
│           │    POST /api/auth/login         │  bcrypt  │
│           │  ──────────────────────────►   │  verify  │
│           │                                │          │
│           │  ◄──────────────────────────   │          │
│           │    JWT token (Bearer)           │          │
│           │                                │          │
│  Attach   │    GET /api/projects           │  JWT     │
│  token to │  ──────────────────────────►   │  verify  │
│  requests │                                │  middleware│
│           │  ◄──────────────────────────   │          │
│           │    Protected data              │          │
└──────────┘                                └──────────┘
  1. User registers with email and password.
  2. Password is hashed with bcrypt before storage.
  3. Email verification is sent via Gmail SMTP (or auto-verified in dev mode).
  4. On login, credentials are verified and a signed JWT is returned.
  5. The frontend stores the JWT in localStorage and attaches it to all subsequent requests via an Axios interceptor.
  6. The backend requireAuth middleware validates the token on protected routes.

docs.title: Request Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
Every API request flows through the following pipeline:

Request → CORS → Body Parser → Auth Middleware → Zod Validation → Controller → Prisma → Response
  1. CORS — Allows requests from the frontend origin.
  2. Body Parser — Parses JSON request bodies.
  3. Auth Middleware — Verifies JWT token (skipped for public routes).
  4. Zod Validation — Validates request body against defined schemas.
  5. Controller — Executes business logic.
  6. Prisma — Performs type-safe database operations.
  7. Response — Returns JSON with appropriate status code.

docs.title: Shared Package
docs.text:
The @logbook/shared package (packages/shared/) contains TypeScript types and Zod schemas consumed by both frontend and backend:

  • Types — Project, Entry, EntryField, TimeSummary, etc.
  • Input types — CreateProjectInput, CreateEntryInput, etc.
  • Auth schemas — registerSchema, loginSchema, verifyEmailSchema, etc.

This eliminates type duplication and ensures both sides of the application agree on data shapes. Changes to a shared type are reflected immediately in both frontend and backend code.

docs.title: Monorepo Structure
docs.text:
coms3011a-logbook-digital-logbook/
├── apps/
│   ├── frontend/      # React SPA (Vite)
│   └── backend/       # Express API (tsx)
├── packages/
│   └── shared/        # @logbook/shared (types + schemas)
├── docs/              # MkDocs documentation
└── package.json       # npm workspaces root

All packages are managed through npm workspaces. Shared dependencies are defined at the workspace root where possible, while package-specific dependencies are defined in each package's package.json.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook uses a PostgreSQL database to store users, projects, project entry formats, and logbook entries.

A key design goal was that different projects need different logbook entry structures (e.g. one project may track "hours worked" and "task completed", while another tracks "description" and "outcome"). Rather than hardcoding a fixed set of columns for logbook entries, we adopted an Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) pattern using ENTRY_FIELD and ENTRY_VALUE. This trades some query simplicity for the flexibility of letting each project define its own entry format without requiring schema changes.

We use UUIDs rather than auto-incrementing integers as primary keys to avoid exposing sequential, guessable IDs and to make it easier to merge or migrate data across environments without ID collisions.

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text:
• USER.email — Unique. Each email can only register once.
  • PROJECT(user_id, name) — Unique. A student cannot have two projects with the same name.
  • ENTRY_VALUE(entry_id, field_id) — Unique. One value per field per entry.
  • ENTRY_FORMAT_VERSION(project_id, version) — Unique. Version numbers increment per project.
  • All foreign keys use ON DELETE CASCADE for full account erasure, except logbook_entries.format_version_id, which uses ON DELETE SET NULL — deleting a snapshot must not destroy entries.

docs.title: User
docs.text:
Represents a student using the Digital Logbook.

A user can have multiple projects and can request multiple password resets over time.

Passwords are stored as a salted hash (password_hash), never as plain text.

Authentication-related columns:

  • is_email_verified, email_verification_token, email_verification_expiry — email ownership is proven before login is allowed. The token is 32 random bytes and expires after one hour.
  • two_factor_secret, is_two_factor_enabled — optional TOTP two-factor authentication. The secret is staged at setup time and only becomes active (is_two_factor_enabled = true) after the user proves their authenticator works. Both columns are nullable / default-false, so they are fully backward compatible.
  • scheduled_deletion_at — reserved for delayed account-deletion jobs.

See apps/backend/AUTHENTICATION.md in the repository for the full authentication design.

docs.title: Project
docs.text:
Represents a separate project belonging to a student.

A project can contain multiple entry fields, format versions, and logbook entries. Archiving sets status = ARCHIVED; entries stay editable either way.

docs.title: Entry Field
docs.text:
Defines the structure of a project's logbook entries.

For example, a project could define fields such as:

  • Description (TEXT)
  • Date (DATE)
  • Hours worked (NUMBER)
  • Task completed (BOOLEAN)

type is enforced at the application layer when validating ENTRY_VALUE.value, since the value itself is stored as a string to support different field types.

Sprint 2 extended the field types beyond the basic four:

Type Meaning TAGS A list of short labels CHECKLIST A list of checkable items LINK A reference to another entry in the same project REFERENCE A reference to an entry in a different project COMPUTED A value derived from other fields via formula rather than typed in

archived_at implements soft retirement: a field dropped from the format stops appearing on new entry forms, but existing values remain readable in old entries. formula is only populated for COMPUTED fields and stores the expression the server evaluates on save.

docs.title: Entry Format Version
docs.text:
An immutable snapshot of a project's entry format, taken whenever the format changes (field added, dropped, renamed, or re-typed).

This is what keeps historical entries readable: each entry pins the format version that was current when it was created (format_version_id), so later format changes never break old entries. Changing a format creates a new snapshot and carries existing entries forward — filling in what it reasonably can — rather than abandoning them.

The snapshot itself is stored as JSONB (fields), which keeps the whole field definition set together and queryable.

docs.title: Logbook Entry
docs.text:
Represents a recorded activity within a project.

An entry stores the date it was recorded (entry_date, user-editable for backdating), the amount of time spent (duration_minutes), an optional deadline (due_date), and its completion state:

  • status — OPEN (work still to do) or DONE.
  • completed_at — timestamp set when the entry is marked done.

Open entries with past due dates surface automatically in the Overdue view and the Open Work page's due-date buckets.

docs.title: Entry Value
docs.text:
Stores the value entered for a particular field of a particular logbook entry.

This allows different projects to have different entry structures.

docs.title: Password Reset
docs.text: Stores a password-reset request for a user. Each record contains a unique, time-limited token sent to the user's email, and an expires_at timestamp so that reset links become invalid after a short period. Tokens are single-use: all of a user's reset records are deleted in the same transaction that updates the password. This supports the US00.3 – Reset Password user story defined in the Development Plan.

docs.title: How changes are applied
docs.text: During development the schema is managed with npx prisma db push (schema → database, no migration history). The single committed SQL migration, prisma/migrations/20260908000000_entry_format_versions.sql, documents the Sprint 2 schema change that introduced rich field types, soft-retired fields, and entry-format snapshots; it is written idempotently (IF NOT EXISTS) so it can be re-run safely.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: The database is a managed PostgreSQL instance hosted on Neon (serverless, autoscaling). The backend connects with Prisma's driver adapter using the DATABASE_URL environment variable; connection strings never leave the environment configuration.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Development of the Digital Logbook follows a structured, dependency-driven approach. User stories are implemented in groups based on the functionality they provide and the dependencies between them.

The development sequence began with authentication and account management, followed by project management, entry format configuration, logbook entry creation, entry browsing, and integration and testing. The Intermediate phase extended the Basic functionality with richer field types, entry-format versioning, computed fields, custom-field analysis, alternative views, unfinished-work tracking, offline capture, and data export/import.

Development was carried out incrementally, with each phase producing functionality that could be integrated with the functionality developed in previous phases.

docs.title: Development Approach
docs.text:
Development was carried out incrementally using the following principles:

  • Implement foundational functionality before dependent functionality.
  • Develop related user stories together where they share functionality.
  • Use the database design and system architecture as the basis for implementation.
  • Test functionality against its user-story acceptance criteria.
  • Integrate frontend, backend, and database components throughout development.
  • Preserve existing project and entry data when implementing operations such as project archiving.
  • Extend existing functionality rather than unnecessarily duplicating functionality.
  • Test new Intermediate functionality together with the existing Basic functionality to identify integration and regression issues.

The project continued to use the Gitea Kanban board, Issues, Labels, Milestones, branches, and pull requests to track development.

docs.title: Development Sequence
docs.text:
The overall development sequence was:

flowchart LR

    A["Phase 1<br/>Authentication"] --> B["Phase 2<br/>Project Management"]

    B --> C["Phase 3<br/>Entry Format Configuration"]

    C --> D["Phase 4<br/>Logbook Entries & Time"]

    D --> E["Phase 5<br/>Entry Browsing & Filtering"]

    E --> F["Phase 6<br/>Integration & Testing"]

    F --> G["Phase 7<br/>Intermediate Features"]

    G --> H["Phase 8<br/>Intermediate Integration & Testing"]

The sequence reflects the dependencies between the user stories. For example, a project must exist before an entry format can be defined for it, and an entry format must exist before a project-specific logbook entry can be created.

The Intermediate phase builds on the completed Basic functionality rather than replacing it.

docs.title: User Stories
docs.text:
• US00.1 – Create an Account
  • US00.2 – Sign In
  • US00.3 – Reset Password
  • US00.4 – Delete Account

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text:
This phase established the account and authentication functionality required to associate logbook data with individual students.

Development included:

  • Creating the account registration interface.
  • Validating registration information.
  • Preventing duplicate accounts.
  • Implementing secure authentication.
  • Associating authenticated users with their projects and entries.
  • Implementing password-reset functionality.
  • Implementing account deletion and the required data-deletion behaviour.
  • Protecting authenticated application functionality from unauthorised access.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: US00.1 and US00.2 formed the foundation for the remaining authentication functionality. Password reset and account deletion depend on the account and authentication infrastructure.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A student can create an account, sign in, reset their password, and delete their account.

docs.title: User Stories
docs.text:
• US01 – Create a Project
  • US05 – Archive a Project

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text:
This phase introduced project management functionality.

Development included:

  • Creating projects with a name and optional description.
  • Associating projects with the authenticated student.
  • Displaying projects in the student's project list.
  • Setting newly created projects as active.
  • Implementing project archiving.
  • Separating active and archived projects in the interface.
  • Ensuring that archiving a project does not delete its entries or historical data.
  • Supporting project unarchiving.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Projects depend on authentication because each project belongs to a student.

US05 extends the project functionality implemented for US01.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A student can create and manage projects, archive completed projects, and retain access to their historical project information.

docs.title: User Story
docs.text: • US02 – Define a Project's Entry Format

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text:
This phase implemented the custom entry structure for each project.

Development included:

  • Providing an interface for defining entry fields.
  • Allowing students to add fields to a project.
  • Allowing field names to be specified.
  • Allowing the value type of each field to be selected.
  • Associating entry fields with their project.
  • Persisting entry-format definitions in the database.
  • Ensuring that different projects can have different entry formats.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
US02 depends on US01 because an entry format must be associated with an existing project.

The resulting entry format is a direct dependency for US03 because the entry creation form uses the fields defined for the selected project.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A student can configure a custom entry format for each project.

docs.title: Phase 4 — Logbook Entry Creation and Time Tracking
User Stories
docs.text:
• US03 – Record a Logbook Entry
  • US04 – Record Time Spent on an Entry

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text:
This phase implemented the core logbook functionality.

Development included:

  • Allowing the student to select a project when creating an entry.
  • Dynamically displaying the fields defined by that project's entry format.
  • Validating entered field values.
  • Saving logbook entries to the database.
  • Recording entry dates and creation information.
  • Associating each entry with the selected project.
  • Allowing students to record time spent on an activity.
  • Persisting recorded time with the entry.
  • Supporting live time tracking.
  • Supporting due dates and overdue identification.
  • Calculating or updating project-level recorded time.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
US03 depends on US01 and US02 because an entry requires an existing project and its entry format.

US04 extends US03 because time spent is recorded as part of a logbook entry.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A student can create project-specific logbook entries using the configured entry format and record the time spent on each entry.

docs.title: User Story
docs.text: • US06 – Browse and Filter My Entries

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text:
This phase provided functionality for reviewing recorded work.

Development included:

  • Displaying the student's logbook entries.
  • Ordering entries chronologically.
  • Displaying the project associated with each entry.
  • Allowing entries to be filtered by project.
  • Providing an entry detail view.
  • Supporting identification of overdue entries.
  • Ensuring that filtering only changes how entries are displayed and does not modify stored data.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: US06 depends on the existence of logbook entries created through US03.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A student can browse their recorded entries, filter them by project, and view individual entry information.

docs.title: Phase 6 — Basic Integration, Testing and Refinement
Development Work
docs.text:
This phase focused on integrating the Basic functionality into a complete application and verifying that the system satisfied the requirements.

Development included:

  • Integrating frontend, backend, and database functionality.
  • Testing API interactions between the frontend and backend.
  • Testing database relationships and data persistence.
  • Testing authentication and access control.
  • Testing user stories against their acceptance criteria.
  • Testing interactions between projects, entry formats, and logbook entries.
  • Testing project archiving without loss of historical data.
  • Validating form input and handling invalid data.
  • Handling application and API errors.
  • Testing responsive layouts and common user interactions.
  • Fixing defects identified during testing.
  • Performing usability and consistency checks.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: An integrated Basic Digital Logbook supporting authentication, project management, custom entry formats, logbook entries, time tracking, and entry browsing.

docs.title: Phase 7 — Intermediate Functionality
docs.text: The Intermediate phase extended the Basic Digital Logbook with additional customisation, analysis, organisation, offline, and data-management functionality.

docs.title: User Stories
docs.text:
• US07 – Rich Field Types
  • US08 – Modify Existing Entry Format
  • US09 – Preserve Previous Entry Format Versions
  • US10 – Computed Fields
  • US11 – Analyse Custom Fields
  • US12 – Alternative Views
  • US13 – Unfinished Work and Due Dates
  • US14 – Capture Entries Offline
  • US15 – Export and Import Logbook Data

docs.title: Development Work
docs.text: Development included the following functionality.

docs.title: US07 — Rich Field Types
docs.text:
The entry-format functionality was extended to support richer types of custom fields beyond the original basic field configuration.

This allows project entry formats to better represent the type of information students need to record.

docs.title: US08 — Modify Existing Entry Format
docs.text:
Existing project entry formats can be modified after they have been created.

The entry-format interface was extended to support changes to the structure of project entries while maintaining the relationship between projects and their entry formats.

docs.title: US09 — Preserve Previous Entry Format Versions
docs.text:
Entry-format changes were implemented with consideration for previously recorded entries.

Previous format information is preserved so that modifying the format does not unnecessarily invalidate historical logbook data.

docs.title: US10 — Computed Fields
docs.text:
Computed fields were introduced to allow supported fields to derive values from other entry information.

This extends the entry format from a purely data-capture structure into a structure that can also provide calculated information.

docs.title: US11 — Analyse Custom Fields
docs.text:
The application was extended to provide statistics and analysis based on custom entry fields.

This provides students with additional ways to understand information recorded in their logbook rather than only displaying individual entries.

docs.title: US12 — Alternative Views
docs.text:
Alternative ways of viewing entries were introduced to make recorded work easier to organise and review.

These views complement the existing chronological and project-filtered entry browsing functionality.

docs.title: US13 — Unfinished Work and Due Dates
docs.text:
The application supports tracking unfinished work and due dates.

Development included functionality for identifying work that has not been completed and distinguishing entries based on their deadline status.

This builds on the due-date functionality established during the Basic development.

docs.title: US14 — Capture Entries Offline
docs.text:
Offline capture functionality was introduced so that students can record logbook information when a connection is temporarily unavailable.

Offline information can be retained and synchronised when connectivity becomes available.

docs.title: US15 — Export and Import Logbook Data
docs.text:
The application supports exporting and importing logbook data.

This provides students with a way to retain, transfer, or restore their logbook information without directly accessing the database.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
The Intermediate functionality builds on the Basic functionality.

The main dependencies are:

  • US07 depends on the existing custom entry-format functionality from US02.
  • US08 and US09 depend on the existing entry-format and entry data structures.
  • US10 depends on the custom field structure and entry data.
  • US11 depends on stored custom-field and entry data.
  • US12 and US13 extend the existing entry browsing and due-date functionality.
  • US14 extends the existing entry-creation functionality.
  • US15 operates on the existing project and entry data.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: The Digital Logbook supports the completed Intermediate functionality while retaining the Basic functionality developed previously.

docs.title: Phase 8 — Intermediate Integration, Testing and Refinement
Development Work
docs.text:
The final Intermediate phase focused on integrating the additional functionality with the existing application.

Development and testing included:

  • Integrating Intermediate frontend functionality with the existing application.
  • Integrating Intermediate backend functionality with the existing database structure.
  • Testing interactions between Basic and Intermediate features.
  • Testing modified entry formats with existing project and entry data.
  • Testing alternative entry views.
  • Testing unfinished and overdue work.
  • Testing offline capture and synchronisation.
  • Testing export and import functionality.
  • Testing custom-field analysis and computed fields.
  • Testing validation and error handling.
  • Performing regression testing against previously implemented functionality.
  • Fixing integration defects identified during development.
  • Reviewing the consistency of the user interface across the expanded application.

docs.title: Documentation and Deployment
docs.text:
The project documentation was also made available online during this phase.

The MkDocs documentation site was deployed using Netlify, and a link to the deployed documentation was added to the project's README.md.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: A fully integrated Digital Logbook containing the Basic and Intermediate functionality, supported by project documentation and testing.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
Each user story was tested against its acceptance criteria after implementation.

Testing included:

Testing Area Purpose Authentication Verify account creation, sign-in, password reset and account deletion Project Management Verify project creation, ownership and archiving Entry Formats Verify that project-specific fields can be created, modified and stored Rich Field Types Verify that supported field types behave correctly Entry Versions Verify that changes to formats preserve relevant historical information Computed Fields Verify calculated field behaviour Custom-Field Analysis Verify statistics and analysis using custom entry data Logbook Entries Verify that entries use the correct project entry format Time Tracking Verify that recorded time is stored and associated with the correct project Entry Browsing Verify chronological display, filtering and entry details Alternative Views Verify that entries can be represented using supported alternative views Due Dates Verify unfinished and overdue work handling Offline Capture Verify that entries can be captured without an active connection and synchronised appropriately Export/Import Verify that logbook data can be exported and imported Integration Verify that frontend, backend and database components work together Validation Verify that invalid or incomplete input is handled correctly Regression Testing Ensure new functionality does not break existing functionality

Testing was performed throughout development rather than being limited to the final phase. This allowed defects in individual components and interactions between features to be identified and corrected during implementation.

docs.title: Definition of Done
docs.text:
A user story is considered complete when:

  • Its acceptance criteria have been implemented.
  • The required frontend functionality is available.
  • The required backend functionality is implemented where applicable.
  • Data is correctly persisted in the database where applicable.
  • Input validation and relevant error handling are implemented.
  • The functionality has been tested successfully.
  • The implementation integrates correctly with existing functionality.
  • New functionality does not introduce known critical regressions.
  • The functionality is represented appropriately in the project documentation.

For the Intermediate phase, the Definition of Done also required the new functionality to work with the existing Basic Digital Logbook rather than functioning as isolated features.

docs.title: Development Summary
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook was developed incrementally from foundational functionality to more advanced features.

The Basic development established:

  1. Authentication and account management.
  2. Project management.
  3. Custom project entry formats.
  4. Logbook entry creation.
  5. Time tracking.
  6. Entry browsing and filtering.
  7. Integration and testing.

The Intermediate development then extended the system with:

  1. Rich field types.
  2. Entry-format modification.
  3. Entry-format version preservation.
  4. Computed fields.
  5. Custom-field analysis.
  6. Alternative entry views.
  7. Unfinished-work and due-date functionality.
  8. Offline entry capture and synchronisation.
  9. Data export and import.
  10. Integration and regression testing.

This dependency-driven approach allowed each phase to build on previously completed functionality while reducing the risk of breaking existing project and entry data.

The completed development plan therefore reflects the progression from the foundational Digital Logbook requirements to the expanded Intermediate functionality while maintaining the original system architecture and project structure.

Implementation sequence:

  1. Define reusable data queries and transformations for custom-field analysis.
  2. Add charts or comparison displays without hard-coded field names.
  3. Add calendar and board representations while retaining the same underlying entries as the timeline.
  4. Add unfinished/completed state and due-date filtering.
  5. Test each view with multiple projects and field types.

Definition of done: US11–US13 pass without modifying or duplicating the underlying entry records.

docs.title: M5 – Offline access and portable records
docs.text:
Owner: Person 3 – Offline & Data User stories: US14–US15.

Story Planned capability Dependency US14 Save entries locally while offline and synchronise on reconnection M2 entry creation; M3 entry-format data must remain compatible US15 Export a readable backup and import valid data safely M2 projects, fields and entries; M3 versioned formats where included

Implementation sequence:

  1. Store pending entries locally with enough project/field information to retry safely.
  2. Detect reconnection and synchronise without duplicating entries.
  3. Export projects, formats and entries in documented JSON/CSV forms.
  4. Validate imports and report invalid backup data clearly.
  5. Test offline creation, reconnection, duplicate protection, export and restore using a separate test account or database branch.

Definition of done: no entry is lost across a connectivity interruption, and an exported logbook can be read and restored successfully.

docs.title: M6 – Integration, testing and quality
docs.text:
Owner: Person 4 – Integration & Testing, with support from all members.

Goal: prove that independently developed features work together as one logbook.

  • Apply tracked Prisma migrations to the target Neon database.
  • Run backend/API tests, frontend production builds and linting.
  • Test every user-story acceptance table in docs/user-stories/user-stories.md.
  • Test cross-feature flows: rich/versioned formats with offline entries, imported data with views/statistics, and due dates in all entry views.
  • Test authorisation: one student must not access another student's projects, entries or exports.
  • Test error messages, empty states, responsive layouts and regression cases.
  • Record defects, assign an owner, retest fixes and update acceptance status.

Definition of done: all required stories are marked Pass, migrations and deployment configuration are documented, and no known critical defect remains.

docs.title: M7 – Release and demonstration
docs.text:
Goal: deliver a stable, documented version of the agreed product.

  1. Merge approved feature branches into main through pull requests.
  2. Apply production migrations through the agreed integration process.
  3. Verify production configuration, database connectivity and authentication.
  4. Run a final demonstration: account → project → format → entry → review → statistics/due work → offline/export where applicable.
  5. Finalise architecture, setup, roadmap, user-story and testing documentation.
  6. Tag or otherwise identify the submission/release commit.

docs.title: Roadmap completion criteria
docs.text:
The roadmap is complete when:

  • Every agreed user story, US00.1–US15, has passed its acceptance tests.
  • Frontend, backend, database and migrations work together in the target environment.
  • The user can safely create, find, retain, export and restore their record of work.
  • Offline, rich-format, statistics/view and due-date features do not regress Basic logbook behaviour.
  • Documentation, deployment instructions and test evidence are ready for the final demonstration or submission.

docs.title: 1. High-Level System Architecture
docs.text: The Digital Logbook is designed as a non-monolithic web application. The system separates the user interface from the backend API and database.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The system consists of the following main components:

  • Frontend: React, Vite, and TypeScript provide the user interface.
  • Backend: Express and TypeScript provide the hand-written REST API and application logic.
  • Database: PostgreSQL, hosted using Neon, stores persistent data.
  • Prisma: Provides database access from the backend.
  • Authentication: JWT-based authentication protects authenticated API requests.
  • Email Service: Nodemailer supports email verification and password-reset functionality.
  • Shared Package: @logbook/shared contains types and validation schemas shared between the frontend and backend.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
The frontend communicates with the backend using HTTP REST requests. Authenticated requests include a JWT token.

The backend validates incoming requests using Zod before processing business logic and accessing the database through Prisma.

docs.title: 2. Component Architecture
docs.text: The application is divided into separate frontend and backend components. This separation allows the frontend and backend to be developed, tested, and deployed independently.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
The frontend is responsible for the user interface, client-side routing, form interaction, and communication with the backend API.

The main frontend components are:

  • Pages — Application screens such as Dashboard, Projects, Entries, Profile, and Settings.
  • Reusable Components — Shared interface elements such as the Sidebar, forms, modals, and page headers.
  • API Client — Uses Axios to communicate with the backend REST API.
  • Routing — React Router manages public and authenticated routes.

docs.title: Backend
docs.text:
The backend provides the application's hand-written REST API and contains the business logic.

The main backend components are:

  • Routes — Define the HTTP API endpoints.
  • Middleware — Handles authentication and request processing.
  • Validation — Zod schemas validate incoming request data.
  • Controllers — Implement application business logic.
  • Utils — Provide supporting functionality such as password hashing and email delivery.
  • Prisma — Provides access to the PostgreSQL database.

docs.title: Shared Package
docs.text: The @logbook/shared package contains common TypeScript types and Zod schemas used by both the frontend and backend. This reduces duplication and keeps the data structures used across the application consistent.

docs.title: 3. Database Design
docs.text: The Digital Logbook uses PostgreSQL as its persistent data store. Prisma ORM provides access to the database from the Express backend.

docs.title: Main Entities
docs.text: Entity Purpose User Stores student account information Project Stores projects belonging to a student EntryField Defines the custom fields available for a project LogbookEntry Stores individual logbook entries EntryValue Stores the value of a custom field for an entry PasswordReset Stores password-reset information

docs.title: Key Relationships
docs.text:
• A user can own multiple projects.
  • A project can contain multiple entry fields and logbook entries.
  • An entry contains values corresponding to the fields defined by its project.
  • Password-reset records are associated with the user who requested the reset.

docs.title: Data Integrity
docs.text: Foreign keys are used to maintain relationships between entities. Unique constraints prevent duplicate values where required, and cascading deletes support account deletion and associated data removal.

docs.title: Design Goals
docs.text:
The Digital Logbook interface is designed to be:

  • Simple and easy for students to navigate.
  • Responsive across desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.
  • Accessible and readable.
  • Consistent across all pages.
  • Focused on quickly recording and reviewing logbook entries.
  • Flexible enough to support custom entry formats and different field types.
  • Clear when displaying deadlines, overdue work, and unfinished entries.

docs.title: Design Artifacts
docs.text:
The interface was designed using low-fidelity wireframes followed by a higher-fidelity mockup:

  • 📄 Wireframe — initial layout and navigation structure for each screen.
  • 📄 Mockup — refined visual design based on the wireframe.

The implemented interface follows the overall structure established by these design artifacts while incorporating additional functionality introduced during the Intermediate phase.
